quotes/john-damascus-angel-definition/te: An angel, then, is an intelligent essence, in perpetual motion, with free-will, incorporeal, ministering to God, having obtained by grace an immortal nature.
quotes/athanasius-antony-demons/text: In his discourse to the monks, Antony teaches that the demons are not to be feared: they have no power since Christ’s coming, they work through fear and deceit, and they flee at the sign of the cross and at prayer; the discernment of spirits is learned through humility.
quotes/evagrius-eight-thoughts/text: Evagrius teaches that there are eight generic thoughts through which the demons attack — gluttony, lust, avarice, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride — and that the monk must learn to recognise them and answer them with Scripture.
quotes/augustine-angels-fall-pride/text: Augustine teaches that God created all angels good; some turned from God to delight in their own power through pride, so forming the society of the devil, while the others held fast to God — two societies of angels anticipating the two cities.
quotes/ps-dionysius-nine-orders/text: Dionysius arranges the heavenly beings in three triads: seraphim, cherubim and thrones nearest God; dominions, powers and authorities in the middle; principalities, archangels and angels nearest us — each order purifying, illuminating and perfecting the one below.
quotes/gregory-nine-orders-para/text: Gregory counts nine orders of angels from Scripture — angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim and seraphim — and says the names describe their ministries, not their natures.
quotes/basil-guardian-angel-para/text: Basil teaches that beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd, guiding him toward life — unless sin drives the angel away.
quotes/aquinas-angels-para/text: Aquinas teaches that angels are pure intellectual creatures without bodies, each a species to itself; they were created in grace, and those who sinned did so by pride, desiring to be like God by their own power, in their first moment of choice — a choice that is irrevocable.
quotes/kramer-malleus-para/text: The Malleus argues that denying the reality of witchcraft is itself heretical, that witches act through a pact with the devil, and — in its most notorious section — that women are more prone to witchcraft because of supposed weakness of faith and carnal desire.
quotes/luther-ancient-foe/text: For still our ancient foe / Doth seek to work us woe; / His craft and power are great, / And armed with cruel hate, / On earth is not his equal.
quotes/spee-cautio-para/text: Spee argues that under torture the innocent will confess anything, and that if the same procedures were applied to judges, priests or the pope, they too would confess to witchcraft; the trials therefore create the very witches they claim to discover.
quotes/bekker-para/text: Bekker argues that Scripture, rightly read, gives the devil no power to act in the bodily world, so that possession, pacts and witches’ flights are human fictions that dishonour God’s sole sovereignty.
quotes/mather-ten-witches/text: It were better that ten suspected witches should escape, than that one innocent person should be condemned.
quotes/bultmann-myth-para/text: Bultmann argues that modern people who use electric light and medicine cannot also believe in a New Testament world of spirits and demons; the kerygma must be freed from this mythological framework and interpreted existentially as a call to authentic existence.
quotes/lewis-two-errors-para/text: In his preface Lewis warns of two equal and opposite errors about devils: to disbelieve in their existence, or to believe and feel an excessive and unhealthy interest in them — and the devils are pleased by both.
quotes/wink-powers-para/text: Wink argues that the “principalities and powers” are the inner spirituality of outer structures — nations, corporations, institutions — which are good, fallen and redeemable at once; the gospel calls the powers back to their divine vocation through nonviolent resistance.
quotes/wagner-territorial-para/text: Wagner argues that Satan assigns high-ranking demons to nations, cities and peoples, as with the “prince of Persia” in Daniel 10; evangelism advances when believers identify these territorial spirits through spiritual mapping and bind them in strategic intercession.
quotes/prince-deliverance-para/text: Prince argues that Jesus’ ministry was one-third deliverance, that the Greek term often translated “possessed” means “demonised”, and that Christians can be oppressed by demons in areas of their lives and need deliverance through renouncing sin and commanding spirits to leave.
quotes/bediako-christ-victor-africa/text: Bediako argues that in African experience the gospel is received as the victory of Christ over all spiritual powers — ancestors, spirits and witchcraft — so that Christ becomes the supreme ancestor and protector, freeing believers from fear.
quotes/macarthur-strange-fire-para/text: MacArthur argues that the charismatic movement’s claims of ongoing revelation, healing and spiritual warfare techniques depart from the sufficiency of Scripture and expose believers to deception.
quotes/pope-francis-devil-para/text: Pope Francis writes that the devil should not be thought of as a myth, a symbol or an idea, but as a personal being who assails us; such a mistake leads us to let down our guard.
quotes/irenaeus-recapitulation/text: When He became incarnate, and was made man, He commenced afresh the long line of human beings, and furnished us, in a brief, comprehensive manner, with salvation; so that what we had lost in Adam—namely, to be according to the image and likeness of God—that we might recover in Christ Jesus.
quotes/irenaeus-redeeming-blood/text: The mighty Word, and very man, who, redeeming us by His own blood in a manner consonant to reason, gave Himself as a redemption for those who had been led into captivity.
quotes/origen-ransom-to-devil/text: Origen asks to whom Christ gave his life as a ransom (Matt 20:28) and answers that it could not be to God; it was paid to the evil one who held us captive until the soul of Jesus was given for us — though death could not hold it.
quotes/nyssa-fishhook/text: Gregory explains that the Deity was hidden under the veil of human flesh so that the enemy, seeing only the bait of flesh, swallowed the hook of divinity, and so life entered the house of death and destroyed it — a just "deception" that benefits even the deceiver.
quotes/nazianzen-to-whom-ransom/text: Gregory of Nazianzus asks to whom the blood was offered: not to the evil one, which would be an outrage, nor strictly to the Father, who did not demand it; rather the Father accepts it for the sake of the economy, because humanity had to be sanctified by the humanity of God.
quotes/nazianzen-unassumed-unhealed/text: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.
quotes/athanasius-death-of-all/text: The death of all was accomplished in the Lord’s body; yet, moreover, because the Word was in it, death and corruption were in the same act utterly abolished.
quotes/chrysostom-paschal-homily/text: The Paschal homily read at every Orthodox Easter proclaims that Hell was embittered when it met Christ below: it took a body and met God; Christ is risen and the demons are fallen, and life reigns.
quotes/anselm-satisfaction-owed/text: Therefore, every one who sins ought to pay back the honor of which he has robbed God; and this is the satisfaction which every sinner owes to God.
quotes/anselm-god-man/text: If it be necessary, therefore, as it appears, that the heavenly kingdom be made up of men, and this cannot be effected unless the aforesaid satisfaction be made, which none but God can make and none but man ought to make, it is necessary for the God-man to make it.
quotes/abelard-love-kindled/text: Abelard argues that no ransom could be owed to the devil, and that it would be cruel for God to demand innocent blood; rather, by persevering to death in teaching us by word and example, Christ binds us to himself by love, so that our redemption is that greater love kindled in us by his passion.
quotes/bernard-against-abelard/text: Bernard protests that Abelard reduces the work of Christ to an example of love, and replies that Christ not only taught righteousness but gave it, not only showed love but redeemed us from the power of darkness.
quotes/aquinas-superabundant-satisfactio: Aquinas teaches that Christ’s passion was not only sufficient but a superabundant satisfaction for the sins of the human race, because of the greatness of his love, the dignity of his life as God and man, and the extent of his suffering.
quotes/luther-greatest-sinner/text: Commenting on Galatians 3:13, Luther says that Christ, innocent in himself, took upon his own body all the sins of all people and so became, by imputation, the greatest sinner, bearing our curse so that we might be free of it.
quotes/calvin-curse-and-love/text: Calvin teaches that Christ took on himself the curse and punishment due to us, appeasing God’s just wrath — yet, following Augustine, insists that God’s love for us came first and was the cause, not the result, of reconciliation.
quotes/owen-triple-choice/text: The Father imposed his wrath due unto, and the Son underwent punishment for, either: 1. All the sins of all men. 2. All the sins of some men; or, 3. Some sins of all men.
quotes/socinus-no-satisfaction/text: Socinus argues that if a debt is fully paid by a substitute it is not freely forgiven, and if it is forgiven it need not be paid; Scripture says God forgives freely, so Christ saves as revealer, example and exalted Lord, not as one satisfying justice.
quotes/grotius-rector/text: Grotius presents God as ruler (rector) rather than offended creditor: he may relax the penalty of his law, but to uphold moral government and deter sin he set forth Christ’s suffering as a public example of what sin deserves.
quotes/hodge-satisfaction-justice/text: Hodge argues that Christ’s work was a true satisfaction of divine justice: he obeyed the law and bore its penalty as the substitute of his people, so that God remains just in justifying the ungodly.
quotes/campbell-perfect-amen/text: A perfect Amen in humanity to the judgment of God on the sin of man.
quotes/campbell-filial/text: Campbell holds that the atonement must be understood from the Father’s heart: Christ, in our humanity, confessed our sin and responded to the Father as a perfect Son, and his work reveals and opens to us a filial relationship rather than a merely legal standing.
quotes/aulen-classic-type/text: Aulén argues that the "classic" idea of the atonement — God himself in Christ fighting and triumphing over the tyrants of sin, death and the devil — is the dominant view of the New Testament and the fathers, recovered by Luther, and distinct from both the Latin and the subjective types.
quotes/girard-scapegoat/text: Girard argues that human cultures are founded on the collective murder of scapegoats, disguised as sacred necessity; the Gospels expose this mechanism from the side of the innocent victim, and Christ’s death ends sacrificial violence rather than satisfying divine violence.
quotes/weaver-narrative-cv/text: Weaver proposes a "narrative Christus Victor": Jesus’ death is the consequence of his confrontation with the powers, not something God required, and the resurrection is God’s victory over them — an atonement without divinely sanctioned violence.
